extracted_by: hand, T-0294 — the Democrat read, December 1834
note: Vol. II No. 4, the last number of the year. One Tesseract-fallback column, page 3 column 5, and it is the richest single column in the month: a certified chancery order naming a Court House at Chicago, both of the month's estate auctions, the newspaper agency kept in the county clerk's office, and the note advertisement that documents the rescinded Chicago to Green Bay mail route. All seven claims come from it, which is why none of them is marked interleaved. The rest of the issue is given over to the Illinois and Michigan canal — a ship canal survey with a length, a cost and lock dimensions on page 3 column 2 — and it is NOT claimed: the figures there ('9030,020', '74 chains or 23 rode short miles', 'locks 25 feet 1[…] in the cham[ber]') are cut across an interleave and cannot be read with the confidence a number needs. No post-office letter list of any office stands in this issue.

claims.notes: THERE IS A COURT HOUSE AT CHICAGO IN DECEMBER 1834, AND THE COUNTY COURT SAYS SO IN ITS OWN ORDER. 'to be holden in the Court House at Chicago, on the fourteenth day of May next' is the first naming of that building anywhere in this corpus, and it comes from the strongest kind of witness a newspaper can carry — not an advertiser's description of his own premises but a certified copy of a circuit court order, attested by the clerk. Read it for exactly what it says: the court expects to sit in a building called the Court House in May 1835, seven weeks before the scene date. It does NOT say where the building stands, what it is built of, or that it stood finished in December — all three are absent and none is inferred. The clerk's aside is the second fact and it cuts the other way: 'the Clerks private seal, no seal of office being provided' means Cook county in its sixth year still had no seal for its circuit court, which is a measure of how lightly furnished the institution was. The column is this issue's one Tesseract-fallback column and runs unbroken, which is why the order can be quoted at length; the right-hand margin of every line carries a few characters bled in from the neighbouring column and they are left in the quote exactly as transcribed.

claims.notes: BATES' AUCTION ROOM IS A NAMED, INDOOR, PUBLIC PLACE IN THIS TOWN. Two separate estate sales in this issue are appointed there for the same morning — Daniel Outhet's and David Laughton's, both at 10 o'clock on Wednesday 31 December — which makes it a room the town used rather than a phrase in one notice. It is the auctioneer John Bates Jr's own premises (c004 below), and it is the third auction business this month's reading has documented, after David Carver's on South Water Street (1834-12-03 c010) and Garrett's near the bridge (1834-12-17 c001). Nothing here places the room and no street is asserted for it. The six months' credit on sums over five dollars is worth keeping as a fact about how a frontier auction was actually settled.

claims.notes: THE SECOND ESTATE SOLD IN THE SAME ROOM ON THE SAME MORNING. Laughton's sale and Outhet's are advertised side by side, in identical words, by the same public administrator, for ten o'clock on 31 December. Two households' entire stock and furniture going under the hammer in one morning is the kind of event that fills a room, and it corroborates Bates' Auction Room as a place with capacity rather than a shopfront. Both men died in or before November 1834; the estates are handled by the county's public administrator rather than by family, which the notices say plainly by naming no next of kin.

claims.notes: THE CHICAGO TO GREEN BAY MAIL ROUTE EXISTED, AND WAS RESCINDED — STATED IN PUBLIC BY A CREDITOR WITH EVERY REASON TO GET IT RIGHT. This spiteful little advertisement has run since November (1834-11-05 c005) and this is the first printing legible enough to read whole. Three facts come out of it that the reconstruction can use. First, the route: Chicago to Green Bay, carried under contract, and cancelled by the department before the end of 1834 — the same route whose note is the subject here and which the 1834-12-17 issue mentions again. Second, John T. Temple in a role the corpus had not held for him: a Post Office Department letter writer turned mail contractor, beside the three-storey store house with a wharf attached that he lets on the river (1834-11-12 c010). Third, John Bates Jr describes himself as 'an old resident and Auctioneer for town of Chicago', which is the proprietor of Bates' Auction Room (c002) naming his own trade and his own standing. Temple's counter-notice, 'Avoid Imposition!', stands eight lines below in the same column and denies the debt — both stand, with their dates, and neither is preferred. No business record is minted from Bates's signature here: the gazetteer already carries 'J. Bates jr., Auction Store' and 'Bates' Auction Room' (c002 above), and a third spelling of one auctioneer's premises is the firm-identity problem T-0304 records, not a new storefront.

claims.notes: A NEWSPAPER AGENCY KEPT INSIDE ANOTHER MAN'S OFFICE. R. Stewart is already in this corpus as the secretary who signs the Lyceum notice (1834-12-03, page 3 column 1, line 2938); here he takes eastern subscriptions at 'Col. Hamilton's office'. Colonel Richard J. Hamilton is the clerk of the Cook Circuit Court and of the county court, who attests the estray appraisal of 1834-12-17 (c005 there) and certifies the chancery order in this issue (c001) — so his office is a room that holds the county's records, receives subscriptions to the New York American, and is used as a public address by a man who does not work there. That is a real and unusual placement: a business whose whole premises are a corner of a public office. No street is given for it and none is supplied.

claims.notes: WHAT A DEARBORN STREET GROCER HAD IN STOCK THE WEEK BEFORE CHRISTMAS. Wilson & Co's dry-goods advertisement is elsewhere (1834-12-03 c009); this is the provisions list and it is a different kind of fact — the actual food on sale in the town in December 1834. Cranberries, mackerel and white fish beside flour, oats, corn and vinegar is a lake-and-marsh diet with imported staples, which is what a port on a wet prairie would eat. The street repeats and corroborates the December 3 reading.

claims.notes: TIMBER IS BEING CUT OFF OTHER MEN'S LAND FAST ENOUGH THAT THE OWNERS ADVERTISE AGAINST IT. This is the fourth such caution this corpus has taken in two months — after H. Pearsons's, S. C. George's November printing, and the Fox River one — and the repetition is the claim: standing timber near Chicago in 1834 is a scarce, guarded resource, and the town's building material was being taken from quarter-sections whose owners lived elsewhere. Both parcels here are described by township and range rather than by any local name, so neither is placed on the model's ground; what is usable is the pressure, not the location. The trailing characters bled in from the neighbouring column at the line ends are left in the quote as transcribed.
